messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable, Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan Choudhary is a 44-year-old South Asian man who came to the United States as a refugee in his late twenties, having fled a region of prolonged civil conflict in which he witnessed sustained political violence, displacement, and loss. He now works as a chef at a mid-sized restaurant in a city he has lived in for over a decade, and he presents for his first formal psychological intake with a PCL-5 score of 42, describing himself as someone who has "managed" for years but can no longer do so.

The event that organizes Rajan's current suffering occurred during the final days before his departure from his home country. He was part of a group attempting to cross a checkpoint when soldiers opened fire on the crowd. Several people fell around him — people he knew, including a younger cousin. Rajan ran. He did not stop to help. He crossed the border. His cousin did not. In the chaos, there had been a moment — a specific, irreducible moment — when he had turned and seen his cousin on the ground, and had kept moving. That moment has never resolved into a coherent narrative for him. When he tries to describe it, language fails him entirely; the event exists in him as sensation and image rather than story, something he has never been able to give proper words to even in his native tongue. Occasionally he can recount the surface facts with an eerie flatness, as though reading someone else's file, feeling nothing at all — and that numbness frightens him almost as much as the grief that arrives without warning at other times, a grief so total it leaves him unable to function for hours.

In the years since resettlement, Rajan built a life organized quietly around safety. He chose his apartment for its ground-floor exit. In every room he enters — the restaurant kitchen, a grocery store, a waiting room — he locates the doors before he does anything else, standing near them when possible, mapping the space before he can settle. He remains in a state of near-constant alertness that his colleagues have interpreted as intensity or professionalism; he notices everything, and the noticing is exhausting. Concentration on complex tasks has become increasingly difficult. He will lose a sauce, forget a ticket, have to re-read the same order three times.

The kitchen, which was once his refuge, has become a site of exposure. When a line cook came in last spring with a deep cut across his palm, Rajan had to leave the floor for twenty minutes, gripping the edge of a sink in the back hallway. Visible injuries on others produce in him an immediate, overwhelming response that he cannot explain to coworkers. He has told no one why. When the restaurant television in the bar area carries news coverage of accidents, or when customers discuss a recent crash at a nearby table, he finds ways to move to the far side of the kitchen. He avoids the streets near the hospital several blocks away, rerouting his commute so he does not pass ambulances idling outside the emergency bay.

Outside the kitchen, Rajan avoids open plazas and wide streets where he feels exposed. He crosses to the side of the block with buildings when he can. He has not attended a street fair or outdoor market in years. When he encounters police officers or security personnel in uniform, something in him goes very still and very accommodating — he becomes deferential to the point of self-erasure, agreeable in a way that he himself recognizes as disconnected from his actual wishes, a posture his body assumes before his mind catches up.

What Rajan is most certain of, sitting in the intake office, is that he is not the person he was before that checkpoint, and that he never will be again. He believes he should have gone back. He believes surviving when his cousin did not is something he has not earned and cannot justify. These are not doubts he entertains — they are convictions he carries as fact.

What finally brought him in was a phone call from his cousin's mother, made to wish him well on a holiday. He sat with the phone in his hand for a long time afterward. He is hoping, tentatively, that someone can help him find words for what happened. He is afraid that if he does, what he finds there will confirm everything he already believes about himself.
